# Developer-control review

<!-- Generated by scripts/developer-control-review.py from docs/developer-control/review.json. Edit the JSON, then run the script. CI checks that every WIT interface is reviewed and that this file matches. -->

Developer ownership and control is the default (IC-175, IC-176). Krate enforces a boundary only where portability, the recipient's permission, OS safety, evidence, the platform, or the law requires it; everything else is the application's choice, and for every enforced boundary a lower-level portable interface is named or its absence is recorded as a gap.

## Justification classes

- **evidence**: a claim about the app must rest on something a check can read
- **legal**: a law or a licence requires it
- **os-safety**: the host, the person's other data and other apps must not be reachable by an app that was not granted them
- **platform**: the operating system offers this one way, and Krate cannot offer another
- **portability**: the same file must run on every host Krate supports, so the shape every host lowers to is fixed
- **recipient-permission**: the person running the app decides what it may reach; the boundary is where they decide

## Summary

- 78 boundaries reviewed, 69 of them WIT interfaces (69 declared under wit/krate).
- 37 compulsory, each with a justification or a recorded gap; 41 optional.
- 6 recorded gaps where the escape hatch does not yet exist or the boundary is narrower than a developer would want.

| `manifest.toml and the capability declaration` | format | what an app declares it needs, so the person can be told before it runs; an undeclared call is denied | everything not declared as a capability: architecture, libraries, data model | declare narrowly; optional capabilities are asked for at feature time (CP2) | yes | recipient-permission |
| `the .krate archive` | format | one container every host opens: fixed core entries, namespaces, ceilings, a versioned profile | what the app is made of; unknown entries survive so a tool may carry its own | unknown entries are ignored by the runtime and kept by the packer | yes | portability |
| `the WebAssembly component contract` | format | that the executable is a component of a declared world importing only krate:* interfaces | the language and toolchain that produced it: anything that emits a valid component is accepted at pack, publish and open | the validator (krate_bundle::judge_bytes) is the whole contract; cargo-component is a default, not a requirement | yes | portability |
| `publisher signing and lineage` | identity | that a signature proves who signed these exact bytes and nothing more, that storage follows verified lineage, and that a fork is visibly a fork | whether to sign at all: an unsigned app runs, labelled | run unsigned; sign with the developer's own offline key, no account | no | -- |
| `the hub (publish, channels, takedowns)` | service | admission of what it will host: the same validator the runtime uses, and a takedown record with an appeal | where to host and distribute: a .krate runs from any URL or file, and the hub is one option | any web host, any file share, a link by hand; the client holds fetched bytes to their address wherever they came from | no | -- |
| `Studio and AI authoring` | workflow | nothing about the app: the authoring pack teaches the contract, and check-app measures the result | the developer edits the source by hand at any point; an AI suggestion, repair or regeneration is a proposal the developer may reject | the bundle carries its source, Cargo.lock and SDK; open it and build without Studio | no | -- |
| `krate port` | workflow | nothing: a read-only porting assistant with honest verdicts | whether to port, what to replace, which dependencies to keep | write the app directly against the SDK | no | -- |
| `resource limits and the permission wall` | runtime | that an app cannot exceed what the person granted or exhaust the machine: memory, entry counts, archive ceilings, denied undeclared calls | everything within the grants | declare what is needed; the wall explains every denial in plain words | yes | os-safety |
| `telemetry` | runtime | that nothing leaves the machine without the person's consent, and what does is anonymous and says why an open failed | an app's own analytics, over the network boundary, declared | none needed: it is opt-in | yes | recipient-permission |

## Gaps

Where a developer's choice is narrower than the principle says it should be. Each is a row above with a gap recorded; none is a rule Krate defends.

- `krate:gfx@0.1.0/canvas2d`: a developer's own GPU renderer goes through krate:gpu, which presents by copying each frame into the canvas through the CPU until the presenter shares its device (K-407); scene3d is software
- `krate:net@0.1.0/sockets`: listening for incoming connections is not offered yet, so an app cannot host a server (IC-935)
- `krate:speech@0.1.0/transcription`: the recogniser reads one model family; another engine means the app ships its own
- `krate:ui@0.1.0/clipboard`: wired on Linux only today; other hosts answer unsupported
- `krate:ui@0.1.0/menu`: set-items answers unsupported on every host (IC-745)
- `the WebAssembly component contract`: the SDK and Studio build with cargo-component only; a developer's own build tool is accepted by the validator but not by the make flow (IC-175: custom build tool)
